Part 2 / User Interface

Find your way around.

Get comfortable with the workspace before you start building.

Read the interface ↓Choose a workspace ↓Arrange your workspace ↓

Read the interface

Identify the editors you will use most.

Windows & Editor Types

Use the Viewport to work with objects, the Outliner to find them, Properties to edit settings, and the Timeline to manage time.

Choose a workspace

Start with Layout. Explore the other workspaces when you need them.

Layout

Start in Layout to arrange objects and review the scene.

Modeling

Use Modeling to edit object geometry.

Sculpting

Use Sculpting to shape organic forms with brushes.

UV Editing

Unwrap a mesh into a flat map for image textures.

Texture Painting

Paint colors and details directly onto a model.

Shading

Build materials by connecting nodes in the Shader Editor.

Animation

Work with the scene, timeline, and animation keyframes together.

Rendering

Review rendered images and animation.

Compositing

Adjust and combine rendered images with nodes.

Geometry Nodes

Generate and arrange geometry procedurally with nodes.

Scripting

Use Python to automate tasks and build tools.

Arrange your workspace

Switch editors, split views, and make room for the task.

Customize

Change an editor type to show the tools you need.

Customize

Split editors to create more views, or join them to simplify the workspace.

Build a clear scene.

Select, transform, and organize the objects you will animate.

Select and transform ↓Manage the scene ↓

Select and transform

Choose an object, then change its position, rotation, or scale.

Object Selection

Select the object you want to work with.

Select/Deselect All

Select or deselect all objects before applying an operation.

Transformation Widgets

Object Properties

Manage the scene

Add objects and keep the scene organized as it grows.

3D Primitives

Add a primitive as the starting point for a new object.

Copy / Paste / Delete Objects

Copy, paste, or delete objects using the demonstrated commands.

Shading Mode

Compare flat and smooth shading on the same shape.

Drag to rotate
Surface shading

Each face has a single normal, so the individual faces remain visible.

Normals at vertices: Flat keeps a separate direction for each adjoining face. Smooth shares a direction across adjoining faces. Orange arrows show the split or shared directions.

Renaming

Give objects clear names so they are easy to find.

Parenting

Parent objects to control them together.

Collections

Hide/Unhide Objects

Hide objects temporarily to make the scene easier to work with.

Duplication

Part 2 / Modeling

Shape your objects.

Understand the mesh, then use a few tools to change its form.

Understand the mesh ↓Select and remove geometry ↓Build and refine forms ↓

Understand the mesh

Work with vertices, edges, and faces in Edit Mode.

What is a mesh?

Vertices are points. Edges connect them. Faces form the surfaces.

Edit-Mode

Press Tab to switch between Object Mode and Edit Mode.

Select Elements

In Edit Mode, use the number-row keys: 1 for vertices, 2 for edges, and 3 for faces.

Select and remove geometry

Choose connected elements and control what you delete.

Edge Loop / Edge Ring Selection

Select connected edges as a loop or ring.

Face Loop Selection

Select a connected loop of faces.

Shortest Path Selection

Select a path between elements using Ctrl-click.

Remove Elements

Choose which geometry to delete.

Remove Elements

Compare the results of deleting vertices, edges, and faces.

Build and refine forms

Use the demonstrations as a reference while you model.

Extrude

Extrude a selected face to extend the form.

Loop Cut

Add an edge loop, then position it.

Inset

Inset a face to create an inner border.

Bevel

Bevel edges to soften corners.

Knife

Cut new edges into the mesh.

Create New Faces from Vertices

Select boundary vertices and press F to create a face.

Merge Vertices

Merge selected vertices into one.

Connect Vertices

Connect selected vertices with an edge.

Subdivision

Subdivide the mesh to add geometry.

Part 2 / Materials

Give surfaces character.

Use light and material properties to make form readable.

Understand surface response ↓Work with materials ↓

Understand surface response

Compare how surfaces reflect and scatter light.

What is shading?

Compare the same cube with edges only, a flat surface, and shading.

PBR (Principled BSDF Shader)

The Principled BSDF combines material properties in one shader.

Explore one material.

Change the surface. Keep the room and lighting fixed.

Sets the surface color. On metals, it also tints reflections.

0

0 is a non-metal; 1 is a metal. Intermediate values blend the two.

0.35

Low values create sharp reflections. High values soften them.

1

Controls reflection strength on non-metals. It has no effect on a fully metallic surface.

Drag the sphere to inspect its reflections.

Work with materials

Create, edit, and assign materials to your objects.

How to create/remove shaders?

Create a material or remove a material assignment.

How to edit shaders?

Edit the material properties and inspect the result.

How to add more materials to one mesh?

Select faces in Edit Mode and assign a material to them.

Part 2 / Animations

Bring the scene to life.

Set keyframes, shape the timing, and connect movement to a path.

Create and edit keyframes ↓Control the movement ↓

Create and edit keyframes

Record a change, then adjust when it happens.

Automatic keyframe creation?

Enable Auto Keying to record supported changes at the current frame.

Manual keyframe creation?

Insert keyframes manually for the properties you want to animate.

Framerate Settings

Set the frame rate before planning your animation timing.

Keyframe Adaptation/Duplication/Removal

Move, duplicate, or delete keyframes to revise the animation.

Keyframe Anything

Animate a property by setting different values at different frames.

Keyframe Anything

Animation can affect lights, cameras, textures, particles, modifiers, and materials.

Control the movement

Choose interpolation, follow a path, and direct an object toward a target.

Keyframes Interpolation

Compare interpolation modes, then select the keyframes you want to change.

Follow Path

Use a path to guide an object’s movement.

Track To

Use Track To to point an object toward a target.
